metadata.title: How to Make Barbie Doll Clothes (Singlet) Easy.
metadata.description:
How to Make Barbie Doll Clothes (Singlet) Easy.
Hello my name is Ajay and I have a passion for Barbie dolls, I like making clothes for them, I donate all my Barbie doll clothes to the salvation army.

Click here for free scrapbooking paper 
http://designsscr.blogspot.com.au/
 

Hi guys 
I hope you guys like this video. Share your creations with us on Facebook to be in one of our videos, or win competitions.
By submitting your photos on Facebook you are giving us permission to use your pictures free of charge.
Thank you to all my subscribers you guys rock. 
I appreciate your comments, negative or positive.

summary.brief: A DIY tutorial shows how to cut a paper pattern, trim stretchy fabric and glue the edges to make a singlet for a Barbie doll, ending with a thank‑you screen.
summary.detailed: The video opens with a purple‑bordered title slide that reads “Krankn Koncepts DIY” and a quick glimpse of six colorful tops on a red surface. The presenter then greets the viewers and explains that they will make a tiny singlet for a Barbie doll. A sheet of white paper is measured to about 8 cm × 20 cm, folded in half twice, and two small triangles are cut to form a pattern. A matching piece of stretchy fabric is cut to the same size, folded, placed over the paper pattern, and trimmed around the shape, producing a fabric shirt. The shirt is opened and a tiny snip is made at each corner. Using a wooden skewer coated with paper‑mâché glue stick, the presenter rolls glue around each corner and pulls the fabric through the corresponding opening, repeating this for all four sides, then reinforces the edges with additional glue. The shirt is turned right‑side‑out, glued down along the edges with the skewer while smoothing it to ensure evenness. After the glue sets slightly, the bottom edge is hemmed: the fabric is folded, the skewer is inserted, and the material is pulled down to create a neat hem, handling the corner sections similarly. The finished singlet is displayed on a Barbie doll. The tutorial concludes with a still image of the doll wearing green and pink clothing, a “Thanks for watching” message, and a final black screen.

action.detailed: Cut a paper pattern, trim a matching piece of stretchy fabric, snip the shirt corners, apply glue with a skewer to pull and secure each corner, then hem the edges by folding and pulling with the skewer to finish the singlet.

summary.brief: The presenter demonstrates how to cut, trim, and glue fabric to make a tiny Barbie singlet.
summary.detailed: The video begins with the presenter cutting an 8 cm × 20 cm piece of paper, folding it in half twice, and cutting two small triangles to create a pattern for a singlet. A piece of stretchy fabric of the same size is folded in half, the paper pattern is placed on it, and excess fabric is trimmed away, leaving a miniature shirt shape. After unfolding, a small notch is cut from each of the four corners. Using a glue stick and a wooden skewer, glue is applied to each corner, the skewer is rolled around the glue and pulled outward to round the corners, and the same technique is repeated for all four sides, pressing the edges together. After the glue sets briefly, the bottom edge is hemmed by folding, pulling with the skewer and securing the hem. The completed singlet is shown on a Barbie doll, and the presenter mentions that the next video will cover making Barbie pants.

summary.brief: A DIY tutorial shows how to craft a miniature Barbie singlet from paper and stretchy fabric.
summary.detailed: The presenter measures a sheet of white paper to about 8 cm × 20 cm, folds it twice, and cuts two triangular notches at the top and bottom to create a singlet pattern. A piece of stretchy fabric of the same size is folded the same way, placed over the paper pattern, and the excess fabric is trimmed to match the shape. After unfolding, small corner triangles are snipped off the fabric. A glue stick is applied to each corner, and a wooden skewer is rolled around the corner and pulled out to secure the fabric, repeating this on all four sides. Additional glue is applied along the edges, the fabric is pressed flat, and the bottom edge is hemmed by pulling the fabric through with the skewer after the glue sets. The finished miniature singlet is displayed on a Barbie doll at the end of the segment.

summary.brief: A person makes a miniature Barbie singlet by cutting, folding, and gluing paper and fabric pieces.
summary.detailed: The creator measures and cuts a white sheet of paper to about 8 cm × 20 cm, folds it in half twice and trims triangular corners to form a singlet pattern. A matching piece of stretchy fabric is cut to the same size, folded similarly, placed over the paper pattern and trimmed so the shape of a shirt remains. The shirt is opened, small snips are made at each corner, then glue stick is applied to the corners; a wooden skewer is rolled around each glued corner and pulled out to attach the fabric to the paper, repeating for all four sides. Additional glue is brushed along the edges, the garment is pressed to ensure even adhesion, then flipped over; after the glue sets the bottom edge is hemmed by pulling the fabric with the skewer and trimming any excess. The segment ends with the crafter holding a bottle of glue and a wooden toothpick, poised to continue.

summary.brief: A pair of hands craft a tiny doll singlet by cutting a paper pattern, trimming fabric, gluing and hemming the edges, then adding openings and aligning a template.
summary.detailed: The segment starts with the maker measuring a white sheet of paper on a purple towel, folding it in half twice, and cutting out two opposite triangular pieces to form a pattern. The pattern is placed on a piece of stretchy white fabric that has been folded in half; the fabric is trimmed around the pattern and then unfolded to reveal a miniature shirt shape. Small cuts are made at each corner of the shirt. A glue stick is applied to a skewer, which is rolled around each corner and pulled out to create a clean hem on all four sides. After a brief drying period, the bottom edge is hemmed by running the skewer with glue along the folded edge and pulling it flat. The hands then position a square paper template on the fabric, press it, flip the fabric to align it again, and use a needle to poke holes and pin the template in place. Throughout, the background shows a purple blanket on the table with several other tiny shirts of various colors and patterns.

action.detailed: Cut a paper pattern, trim a stretchy fabric piece to that pattern, cut the shirt corners, apply glue with a skewer around each edge, pull the edges to form hems, let the glue set, hem the bottom edge, place a paper template on the fabric, press, flip, poke holes and pin the template.

She is using a brown stick to spread glue on the bottom left of the patch. She places her finger on the edge of the patch and sticks it to the sweater. Then she uses the stick to rub the back of the patch.
The glue container can be seen to the top right, and to the left is a blue door.

summary.brief: A woman glues a fabric patch onto a miniature shirt and then adds further fabric details, cuts, and inserts a decorative stone.
summary.detailed: Seated on a purple blanket, the maker dipes a brown wooden stick into a white glue bottle and spreads glue onto the lower‑left corner of a small fabric patch. She presses the patch onto a miniature sweater, uses her finger and the stick to smooth the back of the patch, and then pushes a contrasting black‑and‑white fabric piece through a hole in the garment, pulling it through and repeating with another piece. After applying more glue with the stick, she dabs glue onto a tiny fabric square with a toothpick‑like applicator, cuts a straight line in a fabric strip with a small razor, and finally places a tiny black stone into a folded fabric pocket, positioning it with the same toothpick tool. The work surface remains covered with assorted miniature garments and glue containers.

action.detailed: Spread glue onto the patch with a wooden stick, press the patch onto the shirt, smooth the back with the stick, push fabric pieces through holes in the shirt, apply additional glue, cut a fabric strip with a razor, and insert a tiny black stone into a folded pocket using a toothpick‑like tool.

summary.brief: A woman arranges and attaches tiny fabric pieces to assemble miniature doll clothing on a purple‑covered table.

She points to a mini dress and presses the pocket area with a wooden stick, then handles a gray patterned fabric with a cut‑out, pulling it out and positioning it on the piece she is assembling. summary_sent_to_llm.root_summary: The video opens with a purple‑bordered title slide that reads “Krankn Koncepts DIY” and a quick glimpse of six colorful tops on a red surface. The presenter then greets the viewers and explains that they will make a tiny singlet for a Barbie doll. A sheet of white paper is measured to about 8 cm × 20 cm, folded in half twice, and two small triangles are cut to form a pattern. A matching piece of stretchy fabric is cut to the same size, folded, placed over the paper pattern, and trimmed around the shape, producing a fabric shirt. The shirt is opened and a tiny snip is made at each corner. Using a wooden skewer coated with paper‑mâché glue stick, the presenter rolls glue around each corner and pulls the fabric through the corresponding opening, repeating this for all four sides, then reinforces the edges with additional glue. The shirt is turned right‑side‑out, glued down along the edges with the skewer while smoothing it to ensure evenness. After the glue sets slightly, the bottom edge is hemmed: the fabric is folded, the skewer is inserted, and the material is pulled down to create a neat hem, handling the corner sections similarly. The finished singlet is displayed on a Barbie doll. The tutorial concludes with a still image of the doll wearing green and pink clothing, a “Thanks for watching” message, and a final black screen.

llm.system_prompt:
You evaluate YouTube videos for a video-understanding benchmark.

You will be given an Action100M-style summary of one video: title, description,
a hierarchical GPT-written summary of the whole video, and a deduplicated list
of action labels extracted at multiple levels of the video.

Your job is to judge:

1) DOMAINS — does this video clearly belong to either of these target domains?
   - "kitchen": a person preparing food in a kitchen-like setting
     (cooking, baking, food prep — NOT eating reviews, NOT pet-food prep,
     NOT food-product unboxing, NOT restaurant vlogs).
   - "manipulation": a person performing hand-object manipulation tasks
     with clear physical goals: assembly/disassembly, repair, crafting,
     tool use, packing, sorting. The video must show clear procedural
     manipulation, NOT just incidental hand movement (e.g. a vlog where
     someone holds things while talking does NOT count).
   A video can match neither, one, or both. Be strict — when in doubt,
   say "neither".

2) NUM_DISTINCT_EVENTS — count the number of *semantically distinct*
   sub-events (procedural steps) you see in the action list. Merge
   paraphrases of the same step into one. Ignore generic narration steps
   like "speak to camera" or "display title".

3) IS_GOOD_CANDIDATE — true only if BOTH:
   - at least one target domain matches
   - num_distinct_events > 3 (the video shows a real multi-step procedure)

Always return strict JSON in the requested schema.

judgement.reason: The video belongs to the manipulation domain and contains more than 3 distinct procedural steps.
